title: Two notices, one Monday
note: Fictional claims (SIM numbers). Verify every period against the notice and the current PhilHealth issuance; your unit’s procedure and the authorized reviewer come first.
intro: You are the claims officer. Two notices arrive on Monday morning. SIM-21A is returned: one hemodialysis session’s treatment record has no attending physician signature. SIM-21B is denied as a “duplicate claim.” In the vendor screen, SIM-21B appears twice: one entry says “received,” the other “draft.”

n1.prompt: What do you do first with SIM-21A?

choices.text: Log it, verify the notice’s period, open a chronology, and set an earlier target.
choices.feedback: A return has its own clock: the response period on the notice, not your ordinary filing deadline. The chronology lets anyone understand the case in five minutes, and the internal target leaves time for the correction to come back.

choices.text: Refile it today with the same attachments, to keep it moving and show PhilHealth the unit is responsive.
choices.feedback: Refiling without fixing the stated deficiency sends back the same gap, and it will be returned again. Correct the deficiency through the linked workflow first.
choices.then: You stop, log the notice, and verify the response period: 12 days.

choices.text: Put it in the pile and use your usual filing deadline.
choices.feedback: The ordinary filing clock is the wrong clock for a return. Verify the period stated on the notice.
choices.then: You check the notice: 12 days. You set your target for day 8.

n2.prompt: Who fixes the unsigned treatment record, and how?

choices.text: The attending physician completes it under the correction policy, dated; you review it.
choices.feedback: A return goes to the source owner of the deficiency. A late signature is added with an audit trail; the original record is never written over or backdated.

choices.text: Sign it on the physician’s behalf with your initials beside it, since you know the session happened and time is short.
choices.feedback: That is falsifying a clinical record. Only the physician can sign it, and only under the correction policy.
choices.then: You send it to the attending physician instead.

choices.text: Paste the physician’s scanned signature onto the PDF.
choices.feedback: An image pasted onto a record is not a signature and alters the original. Corrections are added by the owner, with an audit trail.
choices.then: You send it to the attending physician instead.

n3.scene: Now SIM-21B: denied as a duplicate, with a “received” entry and a “draft” entry in the vendor screen.

choices.text: Match the notice to the received entry, then compare the session records.
choices.feedback: A duplicate denial means either the same session was sent twice, often after a timeout, or two distinct sessions were mistaken for one. The claim references and the treatment records decide which.
choices.then: The records show two separate sessions on consecutive days, March 18 and 19 of last month.

choices.text: Submit the draft entry as a new claim to get around the denial.
choices.feedback: Never turn a draft into a new claim to get around a notice. It can create a true duplicate and hides the history from the reviewer.
choices.then: You leave the draft alone and compare the records: two separate sessions on consecutive days.

choices.text: Email the regional office the patient’s full chart and both treatment records, and ask them why it was denied.
choices.feedback: Investigate first; you may not need to ask. A message to the regional office carries the claim reference, the dates, the notice reason, the facts, and one precise question, with only the identifiers it needs, never the full chart.
choices.then: You compare the records yourself: two separate sessions on consecutive days.

n4.prompt: What do you do with SIM-21B now?

choices.text: Chronology and evidence to the authorized reviewer; originals kept as received.
choices.feedback: A denial is an adjudicated decision. The remedy and its period come from the applicable issuance, and the decision to pursue it belongs to the authorized reviewer. Your evidence is what makes the case.

choices.text: Change the session date on one record so the two no longer look alike, and refile.
choices.feedback: That is falsification. The records are already correct; the denial may be wrong, and the remedy is reconsideration or appeal, not altered records.

choices.text: Refile the received claim as if it were new, with a cover note explaining that it is a separate session.
choices.feedback: Never refile a received claim as if it were new. Correct a stated deficiency through the linked workflow; contest a denial through the authorized remedy.

n5.scene: The signed record comes back on day 6 and SIM-21A is refiled on day 7. Checking the log, you see it is the twelfth return this quarter for a missing physician signature.
n5.prompt: What do you do about that?

choices.text: Report it as a quality signal and propose a signature check before claims are assembled.
choices.feedback: Twelve returns for the same missing signature mean a step in the process lets them out. Fixing the step costs less than fixing twelve claims.

choices.text: Text all the physicians a reminder to sign every treatment record on the day, and repeat it every month.
choices.feedback: A reminder helps for a week. A check built into the process catches the gap before submission every time.
Each fix costs time and delays payment. Returns are also a quality signal.

end.title: Where things stand
end.text: SIM-21A was refiled before its deadline with the corrected, dated signature. SIM-21B is with the authorized reviewer, with a chronology and both treatment records. The draft entry is untouched. The unit manager adds a signature check to the end-of-day record review.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A return and a denial are different routes with different clocks. Verify each against the notice.
  • Corrections go to the source owner and are added with an audit trail, never written over, backdated, or signed on someone’s behalf.
  • A duplicate denial needs investigation: claim references and treatment records decide.
  • Never turn a draft into a new claim or refile a received claim as new.
  • Repeated returns are a process problem, not twelve separate problems.

See Validation, return, denial, The chronology and Is it really a duplicate?
